_comment: The explorer's content: 4 stores x 3 phases x 3 depth levels, plus inspector payloads. Edited by the nightly maintenance job. Inspector code strings use lightweight markup: «hl»amber highlight«/hl» (stored memory), «q»cyan«/q» (query/retrieval), «m»violet«/m» (maintenance), «dim»muted«/dim», «del»struck-through«/del».

store.caption: write(m1): append one line to memory/maya.md

1.title: Write it down. Literally.
1.html:
The simplest possible memory: the agent keeps a text file per topic and, when it learns something worth keeping, appends a sentence. Maya mentions her allergy → the agent adds one bullet under ## Preferences.

No database, no index, no infrastructure. A human can open the file and read — or fix — the agent's entire memory.

2.title: Structure comes from the document, not a schema
2.html:
Headings act as a soft schema: ## Preferences, ## People, ## Lessons. The agent writes with the same file-editing tools it uses for code, deciding at write time which section a fact belongs in — that decision is the whole data model.

Most systems keep a small index file (like a MEMORY.md with one line per memory file) that is always loaded, while detail files are loaded on demand. That two-tier trick keeps the always-paid token cost tiny.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html:
This is how Claude Code's memory works: a CLAUDE.md / memory directory of Markdown files the agent edits with ordinary Write and Edit tools. Being plain files buys real properties for free: git history (every memory change is a diff with an author and a date), human auditability, portability across models, and zero write-time latency or embedding cost.

The write policy is pure prompt engineering: instructions tell the model what counts as durable (preferences, corrections, standing constraints) and what doesn't (session trivia). There is no mechanical enforcement — which is both the flexibility and the risk.

retrieve.caption: retrieve(): load the file — or grep for it

1.title: Just read the file
1.html: When Friday's dinner request comes in, the agent reads memory/maya.md into its context. Everything about Maya arrives at once — the allergy, the last booking, the lesson. For one person's file, that's a few hundred tokens. Done.

2.title: Whole-file load, or search when it grows
2.html:
Two modes. Load-always: small, curated files are simply placed in context at session start — retrieval cost zero, but you pay their tokens every call. Search-on-demand: when memory outgrows that, the agent greps across files (grep -ri "allerg" memory/) and reads only matching sections.

Note who does the retrieving: the agent itself, deciding what to search for. This “agentic retrieval” is slower than an index lookup but adapts the query as understanding improves.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html:
Grep is exact lexical match. It finds allerg in “allergic” — but a memory phrased “can't eat peanuts” never matches a search for “allergy”. No ranking either: results come back in file order, and relevance is judged by the model reading them.

In practice this works far beyond intuition — thousands of lines, agentic search with a capable model, sub-second grep — and a school of practitioners argues files+grep should be the default until proven insufficient. The real ceilings: paraphrase (no semantic match), cross-file relationships, and multi-user scale.

maintain.caption: maintain(): the agent rewrites its own notes

1.title: Edit the file, like a person would
1.html: Maya says she and Sam broke up. The agent opens the file and edits it: the “Sam — partner” line becomes “Sam — ex-partner (as of 2026-08-18)”. Maintenance here is just… editing text. The same skill the agent already has.

2.title: Consolidation is a rewrite pass
2.html: Periodically (or when a file gets long), the agent re-reads a file and rewrites it: merging duplicate bullets, tightening wording, moving one-off events into a summarized history, deleting what stopped mattering. This is the file-world's version of what memory researchers call consolidation — and it's an LLM call over the whole file.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Failure modes are distinctive: nothing forces maintenance, so files silently bloat and contradict until someone (agent or human) notices — “memory rot”. But git gives files a superpower no other store has by default: history of the memory itself. git log -p memory/maya.md shows exactly when the agent learned, revised, or deleted each fact — supersession as version control rather than schema.

1.title: One memory, one row
1.html: Instead of a sentence in a file, each memory becomes a row in a table: the text, plus labeled columns — who it's about, what kind it is, when it was learned. Writing a memory means inserting a row. The structure is decided once, up front, in the schema.

2.title: The schema is the write policy, enforced
2.html: Columns like type, subject, created_at, confidence, superseded_by force every memory to answer the same questions at write time. That's the trade against files: less freedom, but the database can now guarantee things — uniqueness constraints stop exact duplicates, foreign keys keep supersession chains consistent.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: SQLite is the pragmatic choice for single-agent memory: one file on disk, zero server, transactional writes, and it's already embedded everywhere. Add FTS5 (built-in full-text index with BM25 ranking) and you get real keyword search; extensions like sqlite-vec even add vector columns — so one file can be a relational, lexical, and vector store. Many desktop agent products ship exactly this.

inspector.label: memories.db — schema + INSERT
inspector.code:
CREATE TABLE memories (
  id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  subject       TEXT NOT NULL,
  type          TEXT CHECK(type IN
                ('semantic','episodic','procedural')),
  text          TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at    TEXT NOT NULL,
  confidence    REAL DEFAULT 1.0,
  superseded_by TEXT REFERENCES memories(id)
);

«hl»INSERT INTO memories VALUES«/hl»
«hl»  ('m1','maya','semantic',«/hl»
«hl»   'Allergic to peanuts (severe).',«/hl»
«hl»   '2026-08-01', 1.0, NULL);«/hl»

retrieve.caption: retrieve(): filter, rank, LIMIT — in milliseconds

1.title: Ask precise questions, get exact answers
1.html: Retrieval is a query: “give me every current fact about Maya” or “her last three bookings, newest first”. The database filters and sorts; only matching rows come back. Fast, exact, and cheap — no model involved in the lookup itself.

2.title: Filters + recency + keyword
2.html: The workhorse patterns: attribute filters (WHERE subject='maya' AND type='semantic' AND superseded_by IS NULL), recency (ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5), and keyword search via the FTS index for free-text queries. The agent — or plain application code — composes these per task. Note the superseded_by IS NULL clause: the schema makes “only current truth” a one-line guarantee.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: FTS5 MATCH is tokenized BM25 — better than grep (stemming, ranking) but still lexical: “can't eat peanuts” won't surface for the query “allergy” unless a word overlaps. What SQL buys that no other substrate does as cheaply: determinism and debuggability. The same query always returns the same rows, retrieval failures reproduce exactly, and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN tells you why. That's why structured stores anchor the “truth layer” even in systems whose recall layer is vectors.

inspector.label: query — before booking Friday's dinner
inspector.code:
«q»SELECT id, type, text FROM memories«/q»
«q»WHERE subject = 'maya'«/q»
«q»  AND superseded_by IS NULL«/q»
«q»ORDER BY created_at DESC;«/q»

maintain.caption: maintain(): UPDATE, supersede, expire — with guarantees

1.title: Change the row, keep the receipt
1.html: When the breakup news arrives, the agent doesn't delete the old fact — it marks it superseded by the new one. Old truth stays on record; queries for “current” facts skip it automatically. Cleanup jobs can also expire rows nobody has touched in months.

2.title: Maintenance as scheduled queries
2.html: Because state is structured, maintenance becomes ordinary jobs: a supersession UPDATE when facts conflict, a TTL sweep (DELETE WHERE type='episodic' AND created_at < date('now','-90 days') — after summarizing them), a dedupe pass over near-identical text. Each policy is a few lines of SQL running on a schedule — testable, loggable, reversible inside a transaction.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: The hard part isn't the SQL — it's detecting that m5 contradicts m3. Nothing in a relational store knows “broke up” negates “partner”; an LLM has to make that judgment at write time, then the database records the outcome. This split is the general pattern across all substrates: models decide, stores enforce. SQL is simply the substrate where the enforcement half is strongest and cheapest.

inspector.label: maintenance transaction — m5 supersedes m3
inspector.code:
«dim»-- LLM judged: m5 contradicts m3«/dim»
BEGIN;
«m»INSERT INTO memories VALUES«/m»
«m»  ('m5','maya','episodic',«/m»
«m»   'Maya: “Sam and I broke up.”',«/m»
«m»   '2026-08-18', 1.0, NULL);«/m»
«m»UPDATE memories SET superseded_by = 'm5'«/m»
«m»WHERE id = 'm3';«/m»
COMMIT;

«dim»-- nightly TTL sweep (after summarization)«/dim»
«dim»DELETE FROM memories WHERE type='episodic'«/dim»
«dim»  AND created_at < date('now','-90 days');«/dim»

store.caption: write(m1): embed the text, upsert the point

1.title: Meaning becomes a location
1.html: An embedding model reads “Allergic to peanuts” and outputs a long list of numbers — a coordinate in a space with hundreds of dimensions. Texts that mean similar things land near each other, whatever words they use. Storing a memory means dropping a point into that space, with the original text attached.

2.title: Embed → upsert → index
2.html:
The write path: extract the memory text, call the embedding model (one network call, a few milliseconds), then upsert {id, vector, payload} into the store. The payload carries the raw text plus metadata — subject, type, timestamp — because the vector itself is one-way: you can't read a fact back out of coordinates.

Behind the scenes the store threads the new point into an index so that later searches don't have to compare against every point.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Decisions that matter here: what unit to embed (a whole conversation? a chunk? one extracted fact? — extracted facts retrieve far more precisely than raw transcript chunks), which model (dimension counts from ~256 to ~3072; bigger ≠ better past a point), and which store — pgvector inside Postgres you already run, or a dedicated engine (Qdrant, Chroma, LanceDB, Milvus, Turbopuffer). The index is typically HNSW, a layered navigable-small-world graph giving approximate nearest-neighbour search in roughly logarithmic time.

retrieve.caption: retrieve(): nearest neighbours to the query's meaning

1.title: Search by meaning, not by words
1.html: The query “find somewhere for dinner Friday” is embedded too — it becomes a point in the same space. The store returns the memories whose points sit closest. This is the superpower: “booked Luna (Italian) for two” is nearby even though it shares almost no words with the query. Paraphrase, synonyms, even other languages — geometry doesn't care.

2.title: k-NN + filters + a similarity score
2.html: The call: embed the query, ask for the top-k nearest points by cosine similarity, optionally pre-filtered by metadata (subject = "maya"). Each hit comes back with a score — useful for cutting off weak matches — and its payload text, which is what actually enters the context window. The vector was only ever the address.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Similarity ≠ relevance: “allergic to peanuts” and “loves peanut butter” embed near each other (same topic!), which is why score thresholds alone are treacherous. Production retrieval is therefore usually hybrid: vector search for recall, BM25 keyword search in parallel, results fused (reciprocal-rank fusion) and passed through a reranker — a small cross-encoder that reads query and candidate together and re-scores properly. And HNSW is approximate: recall ~95–99%, occasionally missing a true neighbour. Speed is bought with certainty.

maintain.caption: maintain(): the store can't read its own points

1.title: Update by replacing the point
1.html: Vectors can't be edited the way text can — to change a memory, you re-embed the new text and overwrite the point by its id. To forget one, you delete its point. The catch: the store has no idea what any point says, so noticing that two points contradict each other is not something it can do by itself.

2.title: An LLM gatekeeper at write time
2.html: The now-standard pattern (popularized by Mem0): before writing a new memory, first search for its own neighbours. If a very similar memory exists, an LLM compares the two and decides — ADD (genuinely new), UPDATE (refines the old one), DELETE/supersede (contradicts it), or NOOP (duplicate). Maintenance happens continuously at the write path, because that's the only moment anything is looking at the content.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Remaining chores: near-duplicate sweeps (pairs above ~0.95 similarity get merged by an LLM), staleness decay (down-weighting scores by age or last-access, since embeddings encode no notion of time), and the operational one — re-embedding migrations: change your embedding model and every stored vector must be regenerated, because two models' spaces are mutually meaningless. Deletes also only tombstone in HNSW; the index needs periodic rebuilds. The pattern holds: the geometry does recall, an LLM does judgment.

inspector.code:
«dim»1. search neighbours of new memory m5:«/dim»
«dim»   0.87  m3  “Sam is Maya's partner.”«/dim»

«dim»2. LLM gate: (m5 vs m3) →«/dim» «m»CONTRADICTS«/m»

«dim»3. apply:«/dim»

«m»  vector: embed("Maya and Sam broke up"),«/m»
«m»  payload: { …, supersedes: "m3" } })«/m»

store.caption: write(m1): extract entities, merge triples into the graph

1.title: Memories become connections
1.html: A graph store doesn't keep sentences — it keeps things and the relationships between them. “Maya is allergic to peanuts” becomes two nodes, Maya and Peanuts, joined by an ALLERGIC_TO edge. Each new memory doesn't pile up beside the others; it wires into what's already known.

2.title: Extraction, resolution, merge
2.html: The write path is the heaviest of the four stores: an LLM reads the utterance, extracts entities and relations, then entity resolution decides whether this “Sam” is the Sam node we already have or someone new. Only then are triples merged. Edges carry provenance (which conversation produced them) and — in temporal graphs — a valid_from timestamp, because relationships have lifespans.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Modern agent-memory graphs (Zep's Graphiti is the reference design) are temporal knowledge graphs with layers: an episode layer storing raw conversation events, an entity layer of resolved nodes and facts extracted from them, and often a community layer of cluster summaries above that. Every fact edge is bitemporal — when it became true in the world vs. when the system learned it. Costs are real: each write is several LLM calls, and extraction errors (bad entity merges) compound structurally.

retrieve.caption: retrieve(): walk outward from what the question touches

1.title: Follow the connections
1.html: To prepare Friday's booking, start at the Maya node and walk her edges: allergic to peanuts, booked Luna before, was partnered with Sam. One hop gathers her world; a second hop reaches things connected to those — answers no similarity search can assemble, because they live in the links, not in any single memory.

2.title: Entry points + traversal
2.html: Real graph retrieval is two-stage: first find entry nodes (by name match or embedding search over node summaries — graphs and vectors compose), then traverse a bounded neighbourhood, collecting current fact edges. The result is a small subgraph rendered as text for the context window. Multi-hop questions — “anything to avoid for Maya's dinner guests?” — are where this wins: Maya → dined-with → Sam → Sam's constraints, in two hops.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Because edges are timestamped, queries filter to invalid_at IS NULL — “what is true now” — or deliberately time-travel (“what did we believe on Aug 10?”). Production systems fuse three searches (semantic embedding, BM25 over facts, graph BFS) and rerank the union. The trade: retrieval is fast and precise, but you paid for it at write time with all that extraction — the mirror image of files, which are free to write and expensive to search well.

«q»WHERE r.invalid_at IS NULL«/q»
«q»RETURN m, r, x«/q»

maintain.caption: maintain(): invalidate the edge, keep the history

1.title: Facts get an end date, not an eraser
1.html: The breakup doesn't delete anything. The PARTNER edge between Maya and Sam gets stamped invalid as of Aug 18 — it stops appearing in “what's true now”, but the graph still remembers that it was true, and when. The past stays queryable; the present stays clean.

2.title: Contradiction handling is built into the write path
2.html: When the new episode “Sam and I broke up” is ingested, extraction produces a fact that conflicts with the existing PARTNER edge between the same two nodes — and that structural collision is exactly what makes the contradiction detectable. An LLM confirms the conflict; the old edge gets invalid_at; the new state is written. This is the graph's signature advantage: supersession is a first-class, schema-level operation.

3.title: Under the hood
3.html: Beyond edge invalidation: community re-summarization (cluster summaries refreshed as their subgraphs change), entity-merge repair (undoing a bad resolution that fused two people — the most painful failure, since edges from both got tangled), and pruning episode layers whose facts have been fully absorbed. Maintenance is the strongest and the most expensive here — the graph structure gives leverage the other stores lack, and demands upkeep they don't need.
